title: Rebasing & History
tagline: Merge preserves exactly what happened; rebase rewrites the story to look like it happened in a cleaner order.

concept.label: What
concept.text: git rebase replays your branch's commits on top of another branch, one by one, instead of merging them in.

concept.label: Why
concept.text: A tangle of merge commits from a long-running branch is hard to read; a rebased branch looks like it was written in a straight line.

concept.label: How
concept.text: git rebase main replays your branch onto main's tip; git rebase -i lets you reorder, squash, or reword commits first.

concept.label: When
concept.text: Cleaning up your OWN local/unpushed commits before opening a pull request -- never on commits others have already pulled.

concept.label: Where
concept.text: Tidying a feature branch before Module 7's pull request, so reviewers see a clean, logical set of commits.

mnemonic.label: Never rebase shared history
mnemonic.text: the one Git rule worth memorising word for word, not just the gist

sandboxNote.text: rebase rewrites commit hashes -- practice on a local branch you haven't pushed, exactly as the Golden Rule below says.

code:
git switch -c messy-feature
echo "v1" > feature.txt && git add . && git commit -m "wip"
echo "v2" > feature.txt && git add . && git commit -m "wip more"
echo "v3" > feature.txt && git add . && git commit -m "actually finish it"

git rebase -i HEAD~3             # interactive: squash the 3 messy commits into 1
# an editor opens -- change "pick" to "squash" (or "s") on the last two lines,
# save, then write ONE clean final commit message

git log --oneline                # now shows 1 clean commit instead of 3 messy ones

git switch main
git rebase messy-feature          # or: replay messy-feature's (now-clean) commit onto main

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: The Golden Rule in the mnemonic isn't a suggestion -- rebasing a branch OTHERS have already pulled rewrites commits they still have the old versions of, and their next pull turns into a mess. Local-only branches are always safe to rebase.

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Make 3 deliberately messy "wip" commits like the example, then squash them with interactive rebase. Read the editor screen carefully before saving -- it's genuinely instructing you, not just showing output.
cycle.hint: If an interactive rebase goes wrong mid-way, git rebase --abort puts you back exactly where you started, no harm done. It's safe to experiment.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: On a real feature branch of your own with several small commits, use interactive rebase to reword at least one commit message and reorder two commits -- not just squash.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: What confused you about the interactive rebase editor the first time? What did pick/squash/reword actually do once you tried each?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. I expected squash to auto-write a combined message -- it actually opens a SECOND editor screen showing both old messages, letting me write the final one myself...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can state the Golden Rule of rebasing from memory.
I squashed 3 messy commits into 1 with interactive rebase.
I used rebase --abort at least once to back out safely.
I reordered and reworded commits on a real branch of mine.
I wrote a reflection note above.
